newsitem.title: USA: PacifiCare warns of shortfall, stock tumbles.
newsitem.headline: PacifiCare warns of shortfall, stock tumbles.

text.p: Shares of PacifiCare Health Systems Inc. fell sharply for the second time in a week Friday after the managed health care company warned that its second-quarter earnings would be less than half of what most analysts were forecasting.

The Cypress, Calif.-based company said a host of problems at newly acquired FHP International Co. would reduce second-quarter net income to around 30 cents to 45 cents per share, compared with $1.15 in the comparable period last year.

The news stunned industry analysts, who as recently as Tuesday had trimmed their estimates by 10 cents to 20 cents to around $1.03 a share in reaction to a less-specific forecast by the company earlier in the week.
Virtually all of the analysts who track the company underestimated the magnitude of the shortfall.

PacifiCare class B shares, which had lost more than 20 percent of their value when the company first warned of weak results on Tuesday, fell another $6.1875 to $62.875 on Nasdaq in late trading. The company's Class A shares, which are not as widely held, fell $6.50 to $59.375, also on Nasdaq.

PacifiCare also predicted a substantial decrease in earnings for 1997 and flat membership growth for the year as it focuses on raising prices to appropriate levels and disposing of some particularly troubled assets.
"We are obviously disappointed by the performance of a number of these newly acquired assets," President Alan Hoops said in a statement.
He added that the integration of PacifiCare with FHP continued to proceed on track and that the company was seeing "tangible results of our integration effort."

PacifiCare agreed late last year to acquire FHP for $2.2 billion and closed the deal in February. The combination created the fifth-largest for-profit health maintenance organisation in the United States.

But PacifiCare said Friday it had not been aware of the magnitude of problems at FHP, where operations in many states were burdened by high medical costs and insufficient premiums. FHP operations in Utah, for instance, are seeing a medical loss ratio close to 100 percent, meaning all the revenue generated is being used just to cover medical costs. In many other markets, the medical loss ratio is running above PacifiCare's traditional level of 85 percent.

PacifiCare said the already struggling FHP operations deteriorated early this year, when completion of the merger was delayed for about a month, causing management to lose focus and claims processing to lag.

PacifiCare has also experienced problems at some of its own operations, especially in its core California business. The company said results in California were hurt by surging prescription drug prices and harsh competition for new enrollees, which has kept premiums in the state close to flat for the past five years.
Although these same problems have plagued much of the managed care industry, the dire warnings from PacifiCare did not have much impact on other HMO company stocks Friday.
"(PacifiCare) took a big bite when they bought FHP," said National Securities analyst Michael LeConey. "The PacifiCare problem is a function of a digestion problem related to the FHP acquisition."

In a conference call with analysts, PacifiCare officers said they had plans underway to correct existing shortfalls by selling particularly troubled operations in Illinois and New Mexico, raising premiums in California and further integrating operations with FHP's to more closely manage drug and other medical costs.
But they stopped short of saying there would not be more bad news in the future.

"At this point we believe we have identified most of the problems," said Chief Financial Officer Wayne Lowell. "I am not going to say we have identified every one, but the lion's share of the problems and the drivers behind them have been identified."
